title: Midterm - Comprehensive
notes: An algorithm is a finite sequence of mathematically rigorous instructions used to solve a class of problems or perform computations.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
According to Donald Knuth, an algorithm must have five important features: finiteness, definiteness, input, output, and effectiveness.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
Finiteness means an algorithm must always terminate after a finite number of steps.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
Definiteness means each step must be precisely defined with rigorous and unambiguous specifications.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
An algorithm has zero or more inputs taken from specified sets of objects, either initially or dynamically.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
An algorithm has one or more outputs with a specified relation to the inputs.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
Effectiveness means operations must be sufficiently basic to be done exactly in finite time using pencil and paper.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
The problem of computing π exactly CANNOT be solved with an algorithm due to its irrational and transcendental nature.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
The problem of computing π approximately CAN be solved with an algorithm using various convergent series.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
Converting a number from decimal to binary representation CAN be solved with an algorithm.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
An algorithm CANNOT have infinitely many steps - this violates the finiteness property.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a mathematical model that defines a set of objects and operations without specifying implementation.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
A data structure is an implementation of an ADT - any ADT may have several data structure implementations.
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
Examples of ADTs include List (implemented as ArrayList), Tree (implemented as AVL Tree), and Set (implemented as Red-Black Tree).
Week 1 - Introduction to DAA.pdf
Runtime is measured in number of steps/operations necessary for an algorithm to complete, not in units of time.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
When counting steps, count each assignment (=, +=), comparison (<, >, ==), and arithmetic operation as one step.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
For a simple loop summing array elements: s=0 (1 step), i=0 (1 step), i<n checked (n+1 times), i++ (n times), s+=A[i] (n times).
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
A nested double loop typically results in quadratic O(n²) complexity when both loops iterate n times.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Asymptotic notation describes how functions grow as the argument approaches infinity.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Big-Θ (Theta) notation provides a tight bound: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) means f grows at the same rate as g, up to constant factors.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Θ(g(n)) = {f(n) | 0 ≤ c₁g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂g(n) for all n > N₀} - sandwiches f between constant multiples of g.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Array element retrieval by index is Θ(1) - constant time, requiring only base_address + index*size_of(type) calculation.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Big-O notation provides an asymptotic upper bound: O(g(n)) = {f(n) | 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n > N₀}.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Big-O does not guarantee a tight bound - n² is O(n³) but this is not the best characterization.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Sequential search (FINDINDEX) in an unsorted array has worst case O(n) - must check all elements.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Binary search in a sorted array achieves O(log n) by halving the search space each iteration.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
We write O(log n) instead of O(log₂ n) because logarithms differ only by constant factors: log_a(n) = log_b(n)/log_b(a).
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Big-Ω (Omega) notation provides an asymptotic lower bound: Ω(g(n)) = {f(n) | 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n > N₀}.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
A function is Θ(g(n)) if and only if it is both O(g(n)) AND Ω(g(n)).
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Little-o notation indicates a non-tight upper bound: f(n) is o(g(n)) means f grows strictly slower than g.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Selection Sort has complexity Θ(n²) because it performs Σ(n-1-i) = ½(n-1)n comparisons regardless of input.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
For a problem P, worst-case complexity is T_P(n) = min over all algorithms A that solve P of (max over inputs of size n of T_A(X)).
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
When describing an algorithm's runtime, we provide an upper bound on the problem's complexity.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Usually when we write O(), we really want Θ() - a tight bound that characterizes exact growth rate.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Growth rates from slowest to fastest: Θ(1) < Θ(log n) < Θ(n) < Θ(n log n) < Θ(n²) < Θ(n³) < Θ(2ⁿ) < Θ(n!).
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Algorithms requiring exponential operations (2ⁿ) are only practical for very small input sizes.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Factorial growth n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ by Stirling's formula - even worse than exponential.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Worst-case efficiency is easiest to estimate and most commonly analyzed - assumes worst performance for each subproblem.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Best-case analysis gives minimum runtime but is less important than worst-case in practice.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Amortized analysis guarantees average performance per operation in worst case for a sequence - not the same as average-case analysis.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Dynamic arrays (ArrayList, vector) double size when full - this gives amortized O(1) insertion despite O(n) resize operations.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
For n insertions with doubling strategy: total cost is (1+2+4+...+n) + n = (2^(k+1)-1) + 2^k = 3n-1, so amortized O(1).
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Increasing array size by 1 each time gives cost Σi + n = ½n² + (5/2)n + 1, so amortized O(n) per insert - very inefficient.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
The n-th Fibonacci number can be computed as F_n = (1/√5)(φⁿ - ψⁿ) where φ = (1+√5)/2 and ψ = (1-√5)/2.
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Recursive Fibonacci calculation is Θ(φⁿ) - exponential, while using the closed form with fast exponentiation is Θ(log n).
Week 2 - Fundamentals of the Analysis of Algorithm Efficiency.pdf
Brute force systematically checks all possible solution candidates to find those satisfying desired properties.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Selection Sort is Θ(n²) with C(n) = Σ Σ 1 = Σ(n-1-i) = ½(n-1)n comparisons.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Bubble Sort compares adjacent elements and exchanges them if out of order, with worst case Θ(n²).
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Bubble Sort requires Θ(n²) comparisons even in best case, making it inefficient compared to Insertion Sort.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Brute force polynomial evaluation at x₀ requires computing each term separately: O(n²) with n multiplications per term.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Horner's Method evaluates polynomials optimally in Θ(n) by rewriting p(x) = (...((aₙx + aₙ₋₁)x + aₙ₋₂)x + ... + a₀).
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Brute force string pattern matching is O(nm) where n is text length and m is pattern length.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Exhaustive search generates all elements of problem domain, selects those satisfying constraints, and finds optimal element.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) asks for shortest route visiting each city exactly once and returning to origin.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
TSP is NP-hard - no polynomial-time algorithm is known and most believe none exists.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Brute force TSP checks all n! possible routes, making it impractical for n > 12.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
The Knapsack Problem finds most valuable subset of items with weights w₁...wₙ and values v₁...vₙ that fit in capacity W.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Exhaustive search for Knapsack generates all 2ⁿ subsets and evaluates each - Ω(2ⁿ) algorithm.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Knapsack Problem is NP-complete - no polynomial algorithm known.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
The Assignment Problem assigns n people to n jobs minimizing total cost C[i,j] - can be solved in polynomial time O(n³).
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Brute force Assignment Problem checks all n! permutations - Hungarian method solves it in O(n³).
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
DFS uses a stack (often implicit via recursion) to track nodes along current path for backtracking.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Graphs can be represented as adjacency lists (good for sparse graphs) or adjacency matrices (good for dense graphs).
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Adjacency matrix: A[i,j] = 1 if edge (i,j) exists, 0 otherwise - can encode weights instead of binary values.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
DFS colors vertices: white (undiscovered), grey (discovered but not finished), black (finished with adjacency list examined).
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
DFS runtime is Θ(V+E) where V is vertices and E is edges - visits each vertex once and examines each edge once.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Breadth-First Search (BFS) proceeds concentrically, visiting all adjacent vertices before moving to next level.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
BFS uses a queue to process vertices in order of distance from source.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
BFS computes shortest path (fewest edges) from source s to each reachable vertex.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
BFS produces a breadth-first tree with root s containing all reachable vertices via shortest paths.
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
BFS runtime is O(V+E) - each vertex enqueued/dequeued once (O(V)), adjacency lists scanned once (O(E)).
Week 3 - Brute Force and Exhaustive Search.pdf
Decrease-and-conquer reduces problem to one smaller subproblem, unlike divide-and-conquer which creates several.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Three variations of decrease-and-conquer: decrease by constant, decrease by constant factor, variable-size decrease.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Decrease by constant includes tail-recursion like computing aⁿ = aⁿ⁻¹·a or n! = (n-1)!·n.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Insertion Sort is decrease-by-constant: sort n elements by sorting first n-1 then inserting nth in correct position.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Insertion Sort is Θ(n²) worst case (reverse sorted input) but Θ(n) best case (already sorted).
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Insertion Sort is an in-place sorting algorithm requiring only O(1) extra space.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Decrease by constant factor: computing aⁿ as (aⁿ/²)² if n even, (a⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾/²)²·a if n odd gives Θ(log n) algorithm.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Binary Search compares target with middle element, then recursively searches left or right half - O(log n).
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Binary Search requires sorted array - best sorting algorithms are Θ(n log n) so some preprocessing is needed.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Binary Search uses three-way comparison: target equals, less than, or greater than middle element.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Variable-size decrease: gcd(m,n) = gcd(n, m mod n) decreases arguments but not by fixed amount or percentage.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Search in generic (unbalanced) BST is variable-size decrease - subtree size unknown but gets smaller each step.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Search in balanced BST is divide-and-conquer since left/right subtrees have approximately equal number of elements.
Week 4 - Decrease and Conquer.pdf
Divide-and-conquer divides problem into several subproblems of same type, ideally equal size, then combines solutions.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Divide-and-conquer typically involves overhead f(n) for subdividing and combining results.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Master Theorem applies to recurrences T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) where a subproblems of size n/b are solved.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Master Theorem Case 1: If f(n) = O(n^d) where d < log_b(a), then T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b(a))).
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Master Theorem Case 2: If f(n) = Θ(n^d) where d = log_b(a), then T(n) = Θ(n^d log n).
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Master Theorem Case 3: If f(n) = Ω(n^d) where d > log_b(a), then T(n) = Θ(f(n)).
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 has a=2, b=2, d=0, so log_b(a)=1 > d, giving T(n) = Θ(n).
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
MergeSort recursively divides array into halves until base case (1 element), then merges sorted halves.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
MergeSort is NOT in-place - requires O(n) temporary memory for merging.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
MergeSort has runtime Θ(n log n) by Master Theorem: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), so d=1 = log_b(a), Case 2.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
QuickSort selects pivot, partitions array into elements ≤ pivot and ≥ pivot, then recursively sorts partitions.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
QuickSort has worst case O(n²) when pivot is always minimum or maximum (creates linked list).
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
QuickSort has average case O(n log n) when pivots are reasonably balanced.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
QuickSort partition: select A[r] as pivot, swap elements < pivot to front, place pivot between partitions.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Optimal QuickSort: T(n) = 2T(⌊n/2⌋) + Θ(n) when pivot is median, giving O(n log n) by Master Theorem.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Worst QuickSort: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(0) + Θ(n) = Σ Θ(i) = Θ(n²) when pivot is always min/max.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
A tree is a connected undirected graph without cycles - rooted trees have special node called root.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Tree terminology: node (element), root (top), child (connected below), parent (connected above), leaf (no children).
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Height of tree is length of longest path from root to any leaf.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Subtree is structure below and including a given node.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Binary Search Tree (BST): each node has left child (smaller keys), right child (larger keys), and optional parent reference.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
BST property: node.left.key < node.key < node.right.key, and each subtree must also be a BST.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
BST can degenerate into linked list if data inserted in sorted order - height becomes n instead of log n.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
BST traversals: in-order (left, root, right), pre-order (root, left, right), post-order (left, right, root).
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Karatsuba multiplication of n-digit numbers uses T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n), giving O(n^(log₂3)) ≈ O(n^1.585) vs O(n²) standard.
Week 5 - Divide and Conquer.pdf
Transform-and-conquer transforms problem to simpler/more convenient form, solves it, then translates back.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Three transform-and-conquer variations: Instance Simplification, Change of Representation, Problem Reduction.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Instance Simplification transforms to simpler instance of same problem.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Change of Representation transforms to different representation of same problem.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Problem Reduction transforms to different problem with known algorithm.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Presorting sorts data first (O(n log n)) to make subsequent algorithms faster - instance simplification.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Comparison-based sorting lower bound is Ω(n log n) proven by decision tree analysis.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
MergeSort and HeapSort achieve Θ(n log n) - asymptotically optimal for comparison-based sorting.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Presorting helps with element uniqueness problem and collision detection by making duplicates adjacent.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Balanced search trees automatically maintain small height during arbitrary insertions and deletions.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Examples of balanced trees: AVL, Red-Black, Scapegoat, 2-3, B-Trees.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL tree is height-balanced BST where heights of every node's children differ by at most 1.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL tree node stores: key, value, height of subtree, left child, right child, optionally parent.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL search is identical to BST search - O(log n) due to balanced height.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL insertion: insert as in BST, then rebalance nodes on path from new node to root.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL balance factor: height(right) - height(left), must be -1, 0, or +1 for balanced node.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL rebalancing identifies first unbalanced node z going up from insertion, then performs rotations.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL rotateLeft: makes right child the new root, old root becomes new left child.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL rotateRight: makes left child the new root, old root becomes new right child.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL double rotation: rotateRight on right child, then rotateLeft on node (or vice versa for left-right case).
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Each AVL rotation is O(1) operation - only rearranges pointers locally.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL insertion is O(log n): O(log n) to find position, O(log n) to rebalance path, O(1) per rotation.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL deletion: delete as in BST, then rebalance path from parent of deleted node to root.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL deletion may require O(log n) rebalancing operations - one per level.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL tree height is O(log n) for n nodes - proven by showing minimum nodes for height h grows exponentially.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
AVL operations: search O(log n), insert O(log n), delete O(log n).
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 tree maintains perfect balance by allowing nodes with 2 or 3 children.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-node holds one key and two links: left (smaller keys), right (larger keys).
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
3-node holds two keys and three links: left (smaller), middle (between keys), right (larger).
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 tree is perfectly balanced: all leaves at same level (distance from root).
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 trees grow bottom-up unlike BSTs which grow top-down.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 search: compare key with node keys, follow appropriate link recursively - O(log n).
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 insert into 2-node: simply add key to make it a 3-node.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 insert into 3-node: temporarily create 4-node, then split by promoting middle key to parent.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 insert causing root split: split root 4-node into three 2-nodes with middle key as new root - increases tree height.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 insertion is O(log n): O(log n) to find position, O(log n) worst case splits propagating up.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 deletion minimum: ensure all nodes on path to minimum are 3-nodes or 4-nodes via transformations.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 deletion transformations: borrow from sibling if possible, otherwise merge with sibling and parent key.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 deletion is O(log n): O(log n) to reach element, O(log n) merges/borrows, O(log n) splits on way up.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 tree height is between log₃(n) and log₂(n) - all operations O(log n).
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
2-3 trees not commonly implemented directly - overhead of tracking 2-node vs 3-node types is expensive.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Red-Black trees are practical implementation of 2-3 trees using color properties on standard BST nodes.
Week 6 - Transform and Conquer.pdf
Binary heap is nearly complete binary tree filled on all levels except possibly lowest (filled left-to-right).
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Max-heap property: every node's value ≥ values of its children.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Min-heap property: every node's value ≤ values of its children.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Heaps implemented as arrays with root at A[1], left child at A[2i], right child at A[2i+1], parent at A[⌊i/2⌋].
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Heap array attributes: A.length (array capacity), A.heap-size (number of elements in heap).
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
A.length should be nearest power of 2 when rounding up from A.heap-size: A.length = 2^⌈log₂(A.heap-size)⌉.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
In max-heap, maximum element is at root A[1]; minimum is not necessarily at last position.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
In min-heap, minimum element is at root A[1].
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Heap operations: Min/Max O(1), Insert O(log n), DeleteMin/DeleteMax O(log n).
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Priority queue is an ADT with insert and remove-min/max operations - often implemented using heap.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
MAX-HEAPIFY maintains heap property by comparing node with children and swapping with larger child if needed.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
MAX-HEAPIFY runtime is O(log n) - at most one swap per level going down the tree.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
BUILD-MAX-HEAP calls MAX-HEAPIFY on all non-leaf nodes starting from bottom - appears to be O(n log n).
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
BUILD-MAX-HEAP is actually O(n) not O(n log n) - most nodes have small height so less work.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Tight analysis: BUILD-MAX-HEAP = Σ(h=0 to floor(log n)) ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉·O(h) = O(n·Σ(h/2^h)) = O(n).
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
HeapSort: BUILD-MAX-HEAP, then repeatedly swap root with last element and MAX-HEAPIFY - O(n log n).
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
HeapSort runtime: O(n) for build + n·O(log n) for n deletions = O(n log n) total.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Binary exponentiation (exponentiation by squaring) computes a^n in O(log n) by halving exponent each step.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Binary exponentiation: if n even, a^n = (a^(n/2))²; if n odd, a^n = (a^((n-1)/2))²·a; base case a^0 = 1.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Binary exponentiation processes bits of n from right to left, squaring and multiplying - O(log n) operations.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Space-time tradeoff: using more memory (lookup tables, caching) to decrease computation time.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Hash function properties: accepts any size input, produces fixed size output, efficiently computable.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Simple hash example: sum ASCII codes of all characters, then apply mod m to get index 0 to m-1.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Cryptographic hash function maps arbitrary data to fixed-size bit array (hash value/digest).
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Collision: two distinct inputs producing same hash output - h(x) = h(y) where x ≠ y.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Collision-resistant: computationally infeasible to find two values x ≠ y with h(x) = h(y).
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
By Pigeonhole Principle, collisions must exist since input space is larger than output space.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
No hash functions are proven collision-resistant - we use functions where collisions haven't been found yet.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
MD5 hash function deprecated after collisions were found.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
ADT Dictionary supports: insert(K,V), search(K), delete(K), isEmpty(), clear().
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Hash table combines fast array access with hash function to map large key space to smaller array indices.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Hash table size should be large enough to avoid excessive collisions but not wastefully large.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Good hash function: easy to compute, distributes keys evenly among table cells.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Hash table process: compute h(k) from key k, use h(k) as array index instead of k directly.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Separate chaining (open hashing): each array cell points to linked list of all elements hashing to that index.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Load factor α = n/m where n is number of keys and m is table size - affects hash table efficiency.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
With good hash function and chaining, each linked list has length ≈ n/m, making operations O(1+α).
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Open addressing (closed hashing): all keys stored in table itself, no linked lists - requires m ≥ n.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Linear probing: on collision, check next cell, then next, wrapping to start if needed.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf
Linear probing deletion problem: can't simply remove key as it may break search chain for other keys.
Week 7 - Transform and Conquer; Space and Time Trade-offs.pdf

quiz.question: Which of the following violates Knuth's algorithm properties?
options: An algorithm using only basic operations
quiz.explanation: An algorithm must terminate after finite steps - infinite steps violates finiteness.

quiz.question: Can the problem of computing π exactly be solved algorithmically?
options: No, but it can be approximated
quiz.explanation: π cannot be computed exactly as it's irrational and transcendental, but approximations are possible.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between ADT and data structure?
options: ADT is interface, data structure is implementation
Data structure defines operations, ADT implements them
ADT is always faster than data structure
quiz.explanation: ADT defines what operations exist; data structure defines how they're implemented.

quiz.question: For code with: s=0 (1), for i=0 to n (n+1 comparisons, n increments), s+=A[i] (n), how many steps?
quiz.explanation: 1 + (n+1) + n + n = 3n + 2 steps total.

quiz.question: What does f(n) = Θ(g(n)) mean?
options: f is bounded above by g
f grows at same rate as g
quiz.explanation: Θ means tight bound - f and g grow at same rate up to constant factors.

quiz.question: If f(n) = Θ(g(n)), which is always true?
quiz.explanation: Θ means f is both O(g(n)) AND Ω(g(n)) - bounded above and below.

quiz.question: What is array element access complexity?
quiz.explanation: Array access uses base_address + index*size - constant time calculation.

quiz.question: Binary search on sorted array of size n has complexity:
quiz.explanation: Binary search halves search space each step - logarithmic time.

quiz.question: Selection Sort complexity is:
quiz.explanation: Selection Sort always does ½(n-1)n comparisons = Θ(n²).

quiz.question: What is Insertion Sort BEST case?
quiz.explanation: When array already sorted, Insertion Sort only scans - Θ(n).

quiz.question: Order these by growth rate (slowest first):
options: n, n², log n, n log n
quiz.explanation: Θ(log n) < Θ(n) < Θ(n²) < Θ(2ⁿ) is correct growth order.

quiz.question: Dynamic array with doubling has amortized insertion cost:
quiz.explanation: Total cost for n insertions is 3n-1, giving O(1) amortized per insert.

quiz.question: Increasing array by 1 each time gives amortized cost:
quiz.explanation: Total cost ½n² + O(n), so O(n) amortized per insert - very bad.

quiz.question: Is Traveling Salesman Problem NP-hard?
options: No, solvable in O(n log n)
Yes, but only for large n
quiz.explanation: TSP is NP-hard, brute force checks all n! permutations.

quiz.question: Is Knapsack Problem NP-hard?
options: No, solvable in O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: Knapsack is NP-complete, exhaustive search checks all 2ⁿ subsets.

quiz.question: Is Assignment Problem NP-hard?
quiz.explanation: Assignment Problem solvable in polynomial O(n³) using Hungarian method.

quiz.question: DFS runtime for graph with V vertices and E edges:
quiz.explanation: DFS visits each vertex once and examines each edge once.

quiz.question: BFS finds:
quiz.explanation: BFS finds shortest path measured by number of edges (unweighted).

quiz.question: Which uses queue?
quiz.explanation: BFS uses queue to process vertices level by level.

quiz.question: Binary Search is example of:
quiz.explanation: Binary Search decreases problem size by factor of 2 each step.

quiz.question: gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m mod n) is:
quiz.explanation: Euclidean algorithm decreases by variable amount each step.

quiz.question: Master Theorem: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n has solution:
quiz.explanation: a=2, b=2, d=1, so log_b(a)=1=d, Case 2 gives Θ(n log n).

quiz.question: Master Theorem: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n has solution:
quiz.explanation: a=4, b=2, d=1, so log_b(a)=2>d, Case 1 gives Θ(n²).

quiz.question: Master Theorem: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n² has solution:
quiz.explanation: a=2, b=2, d=2, so log_b(a)=1<d, Case 3 gives Θ(n²).

quiz.question: MergeSort complexity is:
quiz.explanation: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), Master Theorem Case 2 gives Θ(n log n).

quiz.question: Is MergeSort in-place?
options: Yes, uses O(n log n) space
quiz.explanation: MergeSort requires O(n) temporary array for merging.

quiz.question: QuickSort worst case is:
quiz.explanation: When pivot is always min/max, creates T(n) = T(n-1) + Θ(n) = Θ(n²).

quiz.question: QuickSort average case is:
quiz.explanation: With reasonably balanced pivots, average case is O(n log n).

quiz.question: BST can become linked list when:
quiz.explanation: Inserting sorted data into BST creates chain with height n.

quiz.question: What is Instance Simplification?
quiz.explanation: Instance Simplification transforms to simpler instance of same problem.

quiz.question: Presorting is example of:
quiz.explanation: Presorting simplifies the problem instance before solving.

quiz.question: Comparison-based sorting lower bound is:
quiz.explanation: Decision tree analysis proves comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n).

quiz.question: AVL tree maintains:
quiz.explanation: AVL is height-balanced: children heights differ by at most 1.

quiz.question: AVL balance factor is:
quiz.explanation: Balance factor = height(right) - height(left), must be -1, 0, or +1.

quiz.question: AVL rebalancing uses:
quiz.explanation: AVL restores balance using rotateLeft, rotateRight, or double rotations.

quiz.question: AVL rotation complexity is:
quiz.explanation: Each rotation rearranges local pointers in constant time.

quiz.question: AVL insertion complexity is:
quiz.explanation: O(log n) to find position + O(log n) rebalance = O(log n).

quiz.question: AVL tree height for n nodes is:
quiz.explanation: Height-balancing ensures O(log n) height.

quiz.question: 2-3 tree has nodes with:
quiz.explanation: 2-nodes have 2 links, 3-nodes have 3 links.

quiz.question: 2-3 tree is:
quiz.explanation: All leaves at same level - perfectly balanced.

quiz.question: 2-3 tree grows:
quiz.explanation: 2-3 trees grow bottom-up via node splits, unlike top-down BST.

quiz.question: 2-3 tree insertion into 3-node:
quiz.explanation: Temporarily create 4-node, split by promoting middle key to parent.

quiz.question: 2-3 tree height is:
quiz.explanation: Between log₃(n) and log₂(n) - all operations O(log n).

quiz.question: Why aren't 2-3 trees commonly implemented directly?
quiz.explanation: Testing for 2-node vs 3-node adds overhead - Red-Black trees are more practical.

quiz.question: Max-heap property:
quiz.explanation: Max-heap: every node value ≥ values of its children.

quiz.question: In array heap, left child of A[i] is:
quiz.explanation: Left child at A[2i], right at A[2i+1], parent at A[⌊i/2⌋].

quiz.question: Heap Min/Max operation is:
quiz.explanation: Min/Max is at root A[1] - just return it in O(1).

quiz.question: Heap Insert operation is:
quiz.explanation: Insert at end, bubble up to restore heap property - O(log n).

quiz.question: Heap DeleteMin/Max operation is:
quiz.explanation: Replace root with last element, bubble down - O(log n).

quiz.question: BUILD-MAX-HEAP complexity is:
quiz.explanation: Tight analysis shows O(n) not O(n log n) - most nodes have small height.

quiz.question: HeapSort complexity is:
quiz.explanation: O(n) build + n·O(log n) deletions = O(n log n).

quiz.question: Binary exponentiation computes aⁿ in:
quiz.explanation: Halves exponent each step by squaring - O(log n) operations.

quiz.question: Hash function must:
quiz.explanation: Hash maps any size input to fixed size output, efficiently computable.

quiz.question: Hash collision means:
options: Two keys map to same index
quiz.explanation: Collision: h(x) = h(y) where x ≠ y.

quiz.question: Can hash collisions be completely avoided?
quiz.explanation: Input space > output space guarantees collisions exist.

quiz.question: Separate chaining means:
quiz.explanation: Each array index points to list of all elements hashing there.

quiz.question: Load factor α = n/m represents:
options: Keys per table slot on average
quiz.explanation: α = n/m is average list length with n keys and m slots.

quiz.question: Open addressing means:
quiz.explanation: Open addressing stores all keys in table, no lists - requires m ≥ n.

quiz.question: Linear probing:
quiz.explanation: On collision, check next cell, then next, wrapping if needed.

quiz.question: Hash table average case:
quiz.explanation: With good hash function, average case is Θ(1).

quiz.question: Hash table worst case:
quiz.explanation: If all keys hash to same slot, operations take Θ(n).

quiz.question: Hash table vs balanced tree:
options: Hash Θ(1) avg but Θ(n) worst; Tree Θ(log n) always
quiz.explanation: Hash faster on average but unpredictable worst case; trees consistent.

quiz.question: Disadvantage of hashing:
quiz.explanation: Hashing doesn't preserve ordering - can't do range queries or sorted iteration.

quiz.question: B-tree of order m has:
options: At most m children per node
At least m children per node
quiz.explanation: B-tree of order m: max m children, non-leaf has ≥⌈m/2⌉ children.

quiz.question: 2-3 tree is:
quiz.explanation: 2-3 tree allows 2 or 3 children = B-tree of order 3.

quiz.question: When would you choose hashing over balanced tree?
quiz.explanation: Use hashing when only need fast average lookup without ordering requirements.
